cards.explanation: The answer is that he had been a foreigner in a foreign land. Moses had said, “I have been a foreigner in a foreign land.” (Exodus 18:3) That whole sentence got packed into one little boy's name, Gershom. I think that's some serious packing, friends. I can barely get one word to fit on a cookie.

The answer is True. Moses had said, “The God of my father was my helper and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.” (Exodus 18:4) Eliezer, the second son, carries that reason in his name. Try carrying a testimony around every time somebody calls you for dinner.

The answer is that he bows down and kisses him. Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, bowed down and kissed him. (Exodus 18:7) Moses, Israel's leader, walked out to greet Jethro himself, and I love that, friends. Then they greeted each other and went into the tent together.

The answer is False, because the hardships were in the telling. Moses recounted what the LORD had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, all the hardships they had encountered along the way, and how the LORD had delivered them. (Exodus 18:8) The rough stretches made the story, and so did the rescue. I once tried telling a story about a batch and skipped the burnt part. Nobody believed me, because the smoke alarm had already told on me.

The answer is joy. The text says Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the LORD had done for Israel. (Exodus 18:9) He is Moses' father-in-law, and he was happy for them, friends. When good news is true, it can fill a whole tent.

The answer is greater. Jethro says, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods…” (Exodus 18:11) Notice the words “Now I know…” He heard the whole account first, and then he said it. I think that's how you want anybody to reach a conclusion, friends.

The answer is a burnt offering and sacrifices. Jethro brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. (Exodus 18:12) He had just blessed the LORD with his words, and then he brought something with his hands too. Words first, then an offering, and he did both in front of God.

The answer is why Moses sits alone as judge. Jethro asked, “Why do you sit alone as judge, with all the people standing around you from morning till evening?” (Exodus 18:14) He saw all that Moses was doing for the people and put it in one question. It's a fair one, friends. One man, one seat, and a crowd standing around him all day.

The answer is True, and it's Moses' own answer. He replies, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God…” (Exodus 18:15) Then he adds that whenever they have a dispute, it is brought to him to judge. (Exodus 18:16) So that's the whole reason he's sitting there from morning till evening. One man, one seat, and a line that doesn't quit. I've had busy days at the bakery, friends, but that's a different level of busy.

The answer is heavy. Jethro says, “…the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone.” (Exodus 18:18) Heavy is the word he picked. I think anybody who's ever carried too many boxes up the stairs knows what he means, friends.

The answer is False. Jethro doesn't hand the teaching off. He says to Moses, “Teach them the statutes and laws, and show them the way to live and the work they must do.” (Exodus 18:20) That part stays with Moses, friends. The sharing comes later in the plan.

The answer is trustworthy men who fear God. Jethro tells Moses to select capable men, “God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain.” (Exodus 18:21) Capable is the first word. Then he names God-fearing and trustworthy. The list was about character, friends.

The answer is dishonest gain. Jethro describes these men as “…who are averse to dishonest gain.” (Exodus 18:21) That means they want no part of it. These leaders would handle people's disputes, so Jethro wanted men who wouldn't try to profit dishonestly. Think of it as a cookie-box packer who never pockets a cookie, friends.

The answer is any major issue. Jethro says, “Then they can bring you any major issue, but all minor cases they can judge on their own…” (Exodus 18:22) The big ones go up to Moses. The small ones stay with the new leaders. That gives Moses room to breathe, friends.

The answer is endure. Jethro says, “If you follow this advice and God so directs you, then you will be able to endure, and all these people can go home in peace.” (Exodus 18:23) Earlier he warned that Moses and the people would wear themselves out, because the task was too heavy to handle alone. (Exodus 18:18) So the advice is about sharing the load, and it depends on following it and on God's direction.

The answer is False. It wasn't just one tribe. Moses chose capable men from all Israel and made them heads over the people. (Exodus 18:25) They became leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. He looked across the whole people to find them, friends.

The answer is True. The text says, “Then Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own land.” (Exodus 18:27) Jethro came, saw, gave his advice and headed home. He packed a lot into one visit, friends. I've never made a visit that useful.
